title: Cloud Security: An Overview
overview: Analyse a cloud threat by its affected security property, responsible party and relevant control. Apply shared responsibility across service models, then protect data, applications and identities through their lifecycle. Use the lecture’s historical cases to connect prevention with monitoring, audit and recovery rather than assuming a cloud model is inherently secure.
big_ideas: Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud itself, and the customer secures what they put in the cloud. The split shifts with IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Customers always remain responsible for data classification and accountability, even in SaaS.

The CSA 'Treacherous Twelve' threats (data breach, weak IAM, insecure APIs, system vulnerabilities, account hijacking, malicious insiders, APTs, data loss, insufficient due diligence, abuse of cloud services, DoS, shared technology vulnerabilities) can each be analysed with STRIDE and mapped to CSA domains.
Security components split into identity management (users), application security (apps) and data security (data).
Protect data across its lifecycle (create, store, use, share, archive, destroy) and in all states: at rest, in motion and in use.
Who holds the encryption key is the central encryption question; masking and tokenization protect sensitive data that must stay usable.
Access control decisions use actor, function, location and other attributes, enforced through IAM, federated identity and key management.
Manage cloud security by monitoring data and traffic (e.g. CloudWatch), gaining visibility via audit trails (e.g. CloudTrail), and managing access (IAM, SSO).

sections.title: Security threats: motives, types, statistics
sections.summary: Why attackers attack, the main categories of attack, and statistics showing how frequent and costly breaches are.

notes.lead: Know the attacker's motive, then the technique.

items: **SQL injection** → **malicious input** makes a **SQL server leak data**

notes.h: Map attack to the property it breaks
notes.foot: The **quickest way to pick controls** in a scenario.

notes.lead: Cited by the lecture; not a current risk forecast.
notes.foot: Use the figures to **motivate controls**; prioritise **actual assets and threats** rather than treating these percentages as **universal**.

items: **Cited 2019 averages** → **206 days to identify**; **314 days from breach to containment** (the latter **includes detection time**)
**Yahoo** and **Uber** → illustrate the **scale of historical incidents**

items.t: **Reduce the time an intrusion remains active**:

terms.def: Impersonating a trusted sender, usually by email, to trick people into giving sensitive information.
Malware that blocks access to systems or data until a ransom is paid.
Attacker secretly intercepts communication between two parties.
Inserting malicious SQL into inputs so the database reveals or changes data.
Hiding non-DNS traffic inside DNS (port 53) to exfiltrate data.

check.q: A team's security budget goes entirely to preventive controls (firewalls, WAF, hardening), with no log retention or alerting. Using the lecture's figures on time to identify and contain breaches, critique this.

items: **Cited figures**: historical averages of about **206 days to identify** and **314 days** from breach to **containment** (which includes the 206)
**Prevention alone**: leaves no way to **notice** or **investigate** one
**Fix**: move some budget to **retained, protected logs** and **audit trails**, **alerting**, and an **incident response process** → shorten that window

check.q: An online store suffers two incidents: a flood of requests that makes checkout unavailable for an hour, and an attacker on public Wi-Fi intercepting and altering customers' sessions. Which property does each break, and which control addresses each?

items: **Flood** = **denial of service** → an attack on **availability** → **DDoS protection**, **rate limiting**, **autoscaling headroom**
**Interception** = **man-in-the-middle** → breaks **confidentiality** and **integrity** → enforce **TLS end to end**, with **secure cookies** and **certificate validation**
a.foot: **Naming the property first** points to the right control.

check.q: The lecture's figures say most breaches are financially motivated. A startup concludes it should spend its whole security budget on encrypting its database. Is that the right inference?

items: **Financial motive** → protect **valuable data** and the **privileged credentials** that reach it
**Encryption at rest** doesn't stop an attacker who steals an **application or admin credential** that can **decrypt**

items.t: **Prioritise** from the system's actual **assets and risks**
sub: Then **encryption** and **tokenisation** where they cut exposure

visuals.title: Which attack breaks which property
rows: Injected input reads or alters database data

sections.title: Shared responsibility, enterprise concerns and CSA
sections.summary: Explains what changes in the cloud (shared responsibility by service model), lists what enterprises worry about, and introduces the Cloud Security Alliance and its 14-domain guidance.

notes.lead: The provider secures the cloud, the customer secures what is in it.
items: **Cloud security** → like **on-premises security** without **owning facilities and hardware**

notes.lead: Responsibility shifts upward with the service model.
notes.foot: **Data classification** and **access accountability** stay with the **customer**. **Joint controls** still need both sides: the provider runs a **firewall service**, the customer **sets appropriate rules**.

notes.lead: Even when the provider is secure:
CSA guidance groups concerns rather than replacing a threat model. The lecture's chart lists:
notes.foot: It **repeats virtualisation in domains 8 and 13**, so use the chart as the **lecture's taxonomy** rather than a definitive **version-to-domain reference**.

terms.def: Security duties are split between provider (security of the cloud) and customer (security in the cloud), varying by IaaS/PaaS/SaaS.
Cloud Security Alliance: non-profit setting cloud security best practices, guidance and certifications.

check.q: A company moves from IaaS VMs to a SaaS CRM. Which security duties does it stop doing, and which does it keep?

items: **Stops**: **patching and operating** the **OS**, **middleware** and **application**, which the **SaaS provider** now runs
**Keeps**: **data classification**, decisions about **who gets access**, **account management**, **accountability** for its data
a.foot: Moving to SaaS shifts **operations, not accountability**.

check.q: A provider's firewall service worked as designed, but a rule allowing all inbound traffic exposed a database. Who is responsible, and what does this example show?

items: → a **joint control**, where each side owns a different part
a.foot: **Audit and review rules as code** to catch this kind of **misconfiguration**.

check.q: A provider passes every security audit, but a government agency still hesitates to move. Give two concerns that the provider's security can't resolve, and what would address each.

items: **Regulation and legislation** about where data may live and who can access it → **in-country regions** or a **hybrid placement**, with **contract terms**
**Ownership, control and trust** → **key control**, **exit terms** and **audit rights** in the contract
a.foot: Another concern: lack of **in-house cloud skills** → **training** or a **partner**.

sections.title: CSA Treacherous Twelve threats
sections.summary: The lecture’s historical CSA threat list and cases, analysed with STRIDE and linked to relevant security controls.

notes.lead: The historical CSA threat list used in this course; use it as a checklist for threat analysis.
items: **Map** each to the **CSA domains** that address it
**Data breach** → **BitDefender 2015**: credentials stolen from an **AWS-hosted app**, **USD 15,000 ransom** demanded (**information disclosure**)

**Insufficient identity, credential and access management** → cloud credentials **committed to GitHub** were **misused within 36 hours**; possible consequences depend on the **credential's permissions**
**Account hijacking** → an **Amazon XSS bug** let attackers **steal credentials**
**Malicious insiders** → the **'privileged identity gap'**: rein in **shared accounts** and **track user activity**
**Insecure interfaces and APIs** → the **IRS 'Get Transcript' API** leaked **over 300,000 records**
**System vulnerabilities** → **Heartbleed** and **Shellshock** showed **open-source software is not automatically safer**
**Shared technology vulnerabilities** → **VENOM**, a **QEMU floppy-controller buffer overflow**, let one guest **escape to the hypervisor** and **take over the host and its other tenants**
**Shared-platform risk** → **amplified by multi-tenancy**, including **private virtualised environments**
**Data loss** → **Code Spaces** was hacked, **most customer data destroyed**, and the **firm closed**
**Insufficient due diligence** → **Nirvanix** went **bankrupt** and gave customers **under two weeks** to move data
**Advanced persistent threats** → **stealthy, long-running espionage**, e.g. **hundreds of terabytes** taken from **141 organisations**
**Abuse of cloud services** → attackers **rent capacity** from providers who **cannot vet everyone**, and **run DDoS for weeks**

notes.h: Breach vs data loss, hijacking vs insider

terms.def: Historical CSA cloud-threat list used by the lecture for case-based analysis.
Threat model: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
Cross-site scripting: injecting script into a web page to run in other users' browsers, e.g. to steal credentials.
Advanced Persistent Threat: a long-running, stealthy, well-resourced intrusion, often state-backed.
Distributed denial of service: many sources flood a target to make it unavailable.
Breaking out of a guest VM to control the host hypervisor and the other tenants on it.

check.q: A developer commits a cloud access key to a public repository, and it is misused within 36 hours. Using STRIDE, what could happen, and what limits the damage?

sub: **Elevation of privilege** if the role can **grant more access**

items: **Least privilege** → limits **what** the key can do
**Secret scanning** in the **pipeline** → prevents the commit in the first place

check.q: A public API that returns tax records was abused to pull hundreds of thousands of records, as in the IRS 'Get Transcript' case. Which controls would have reduced the risk?

a.lead: Treat the **API as an attack surface**:
items: **Incident response** able to **detect bulk extraction** quickly
a.foot: Any **single control alone** would have left gaps.

check.q: A company chooses a private virtualised cloud 'so we are safe from shared-technology vulnerabilities like VENOM'. Is that reasoning sound?

items: **Multi-tenancy** in **public cloud** amplifies the risk: a **guest escape** to the **hypervisor** can reach **other customers' workloads**
**Private virtualised** environments share the **same class of risk** across their own workloads
Still matter: **patching hypervisors** and **separating high-sensitivity workloads**

check.q: A small storage provider your firm depends on announces it is closing and gives customers two weeks to move their data. What should you have done beforehand?

a.lead: This is the **insufficient due diligence** threat.
items: **Due diligence** on the provider's **financial and operational stability**
**Exit and data-return terms** in the **contract and SLA**
A **tested portability plan** that avoids **deep lock-in**
a.foot: The **Nirvanix** case shows how **short the notice** can be.

check.q: One incident: an outsider steals an admin's password through a phishing page and logs in. Another: a database administrator copies customer records before resigning. Classify each and give the most relevant control.

items: **Phishing then login** = **account hijacking**: an **outsider** takes over a **legitimate account** → **strong multi-factor authentication** and **anomaly detection**
**DBA copying records** = **malicious insider**, who already has **legitimate access** → **least privilege**, **no shared admin accounts**, **activity monitoring**, **prompt deprovisioning**
a.foot: Both are **breaches** (**disclosure**), not **data loss**.

items.detail: BitDefender, mid-2015: customer usernames and passwords stolen via a vulnerability in its public cloud app hosted on AWS; $15,000 ransom demanded.

items.label: Weak IAM

items.label: System vulnerabilities

items.label: Data loss

sections.title: Data security and encryption
sections.summary: Splits cloud security into identity, application and data security, then covers data classification, the data lifecycle, encryption, masking and tokenization.

notes.foot: In the cloud the focus **shifts from infrastructure to data**, because the **customer always owns its data**.

notes.lead: What is it, where is it, how is it protected?
items: **Protection** → **encrypt stored and transmitted data** and **manage keys** (**BYOK/KYOK**)

notes.lead: Encryption is applied per layer, but the key question is who holds the key.
items: **At rest** → **file, volume, object** and **database encryption** (**transparent** or **application-level**)
**Provider holds keys** → **not all threats are covered**
**Consumer holds keys** → it **must protect them**, and the provider may be **unable to process encrypted data**
**Masking** → **changes or hides values** shown to a **viewer** or placed in a **derived dataset**
**Tokenization** → **substitutes a token** and **protects its mapping or recovery mechanism separately**

notes.lead: Deployment model does not decide sensitivity by itself.
items: **Lecture illustration** → **private placement** for **confidential systems**, **public placement** for other workloads
notes.foot: **Public cloud** is **not inherently unsuitable** for **sensitive data**.

terms.term: Data at rest / in motion / in use
terms.def: Stored data, data travelling over a network, and data being processed in memory.
Bring Your Own Key / Keep Your Own Key: customer-supplied or customer-retained keys; actual decryption authority depends on service integration and access policy.
Data Loss Prevention: tools that detect and block sensitive data leaving where it should be.
Making encrypted data unreadable by destroying all usable copies of its encryption keys, subject to retained plaintext and backup copies.
Showing altered values (e.g. XXX) to unauthorised viewers while keeping data usable.
Replacing sensitive values with tokens whose mapping is kept separately and securely.

check.q: Customer support staff need to verify the last 4 digits of a card, and a payments service needs to process refunds. Masking or tokenisation for each?

items: **Support → masking**: the screen shows only the **last 4 digits**, hiding the rest from viewers
**Payments → tokenisation**: systems store and pass a **token**; only the **protected vault** that holds the **mapping** can recover the **real number**
a.foot: Both **reduce exposure** but still need **access controls**, and their **compliance effect** depends on the design.

check.q: A team says its data is safe 'because we use BYOK'. What should you check?

a.lead: Check **who can actually use the key to decrypt**.
items: **BYOK**: the **customer supplies the key**, but the **provider's service** may still use it to **process data** → doesn't prove the provider **can't decrypt**
a.foot: **Customer-held keys** mean the provider may be **unable to process** the encrypted data.

check.q: Encrypted-at-rest customer data leaks through an application endpoint that returned other users' records. Why didn't encryption help, and what would have?

items: **Why encryption didn't help**: the running **application is authorised to decrypt** and read the data → **encryption at rest** protects **stored media**, not **misuse by an authorised process**
**Needed**: **authorisation checks on each record**, **least-privilege data and key permissions**, **access monitoring**
a.foot: Encryption **complements** access control; it doesn't **replace** it.

check.q: A company relies on crypto-shredding to destroy a closed customer's data. What could make it fail?

a.lead: **Crypto-shredding** works only if **no usable decryption keys or plaintext copies** remain.
items: **Plaintext** in **backups**, **logs**, **caches** or **analytics exports** → data still readable
A key that was **replicated elsewhere** → data still readable
**Fix**: apply the **retention policy** and **key destruction** across **every copy**
a.foot: This is why **classification at creation** matters.

steps.label: Use
steps.detail: Data loss prevention, digital rights management, database activity monitoring, web application firewall.

steps.label: Share
steps.detail: Data loss prevention, digital rights management, HTTPS/TLS, VPN, SSH.

steps.label: Destroy
steps.detail: Dispose of data and respect retention requirements. Cryptographic erasure needs all usable key copies removed and separate handling of any plaintext copies.

sections.title: Application, user and access security
sections.summary: How to secure applications (scanning, DevSecOps), users (resource and network protection), the network and hardware layer, and how to make access-control decisions.

notes.foot: The **class sets how strong** the controls need to be.

items: **Adopt DevSecOps** → security **built into delivery** rather than **added at the end**
**Broader DDoS protection** → addresses **resource and network flooding**
**HSM** → **tamper-resistant key operations**, **not immunity** to every attack

notes.lead: Access decisions use actor, function, location and other attributes.

terms.def: Building security checks (scanning, testing) into the DevOps pipeline rather than at the end.
Cloud virtual firewall rules controlling traffic to and from instances.
HTTP-layer firewall for web request filtering; broader network DDoS protection is a separate concern.
Hardware Security Module: tamper-resistant hardware for protected key generation, storage and cryptographic operations.

check.q: An employee tries to download the full customer database at 3 a.m. from a personal laptop in another country. Which access-control attributes should influence the decision, and what is a sensible outcome?

items: **Actor**: is this employee allowed this data?
**Location**: a **personal** rather than **company machine**, and a **country** that may break **data-export rules**
a.foot: **Outcome**: **deny** the request, or require **step-up verification** and limit it to **viewing**; enforce through **IAM** and **federated identity**, not ad-hoc checks.

check.q: A team protects its app with security groups only and asks why it would also need a WAF. What do you tell them?

items: **Security groups**: filter **network connections** by **address and port** → allow any request on an allowed port, including **malicious HTTP payloads** such as **SQL injection**
a.foot: **Layer** them with **host firewalls** and **provider DDoS protection**, because each covers a **different boundary**.

check.q: Security reviews happen only before release, and last quarter a vulnerable base image reached production. What would you change?

items: **Scan** **application code** and **container images** in the **pipeline** on **every build**
**Fail builds** on serious findings → security **built into delivery** rather than checked at the end
a.foot: **Cost**: **slower pipelines** and time spent **triaging false positives**.

check.q: A payments team must protect signing keys so that even a compromised admin can't copy them. Would an HSM meet the requirement, and what does it not guarantee?

items: **HSM**: keeps keys and **cryptographic operations** inside a **tamper-resistant hardware boundary** → keys can be **used but not extracted**
**Not guaranteed**: it doesn't stop a **compromised identity** from **asking the HSM to sign**
a.foot: **Access policy**, **key handling** and **monitoring of HSM use** still matter.

sections.title: Managing cloud security and conclusions
sections.summary: Ongoing security management has three steps (monitor, gain visibility, manage access), with AWS tools as examples, followed by the deck's concluding principles.

notes.foot: Use the **provider's native tooling** for each.

items: **CloudTrail-style** → **audit events** record supported **identity and resource actions**, helping **reconstruct who did what**
**Caveat** → a **log identity** may itself have been **compromised**

notes.lead: The right people, the right resources, at the right times, for the right reasons.

items: **Providers supply** → **network, device, identity and encryption services**
**Secure data** → **in transit, at rest and in use**
**Access control follows classification** across the **whole data lifecycle**

terms.def: AWS monitoring service: metrics, logs, alarms and dashboards for resources.
AWS audit service recording supported account/resource activities; event coverage and retention depend on configuration.
Identity and Access Management: right people, right resources, right time, right reason.
Single Sign-On: one authentication grants access to multiple systems.

check.q: A production database was deleted overnight. Would you look in monitoring metrics or in audit events to find who did it, and what can't the record tell you?

items: **Audit events**: record **identity and resource actions**, such as a **delete call** and the **role or user** that made it
**Monitoring metrics and logs**: show the **symptoms** and **timing**
**Limit**: the record identifies the **identity, not necessarily the person**, because the **credential may have been compromised**
a.foot: Audit logs must be **retained** and **protected from tampering**.

check.q: A contractor left 6 months ago, and their account was used last week to read sensitive files. Which IAM function failed, and what process would prevent it?

a.lead: **Deprovisioning**: access wasn't removed when the person left.
items: Tie **account removal** to the **HR offboarding** process
Prefer **federated identity** or **single sign-on** → disabling one identity removes access **everywhere**
a.foot: **Leftover accounts** are an easy path for **insiders** and **hijackers**.

check.q: A CIO says: 'We moved to the cloud, so the provider handles security now.' Using the deck's conclusions, correct this.

items: **Provider**: secures the **infrastructure** and supplies **network**, **device**, **identity** and **encryption services**
**Shared responsibility**: the **customer always owns its data** and **how it is accessed**
**Focus shifts to data security**: **classify** data, protect it **in transit, at rest and in use**, and control access throughout its **lifecycle**
The **SLA** defines what the provider **actually commits to**

visuals.title: Threat monitoring, identification and management (AWS tools)

steps.label: Monitor
steps.detail: Metrics, logs, alarms and dashboards flag exceptions.

steps.label: Gain visibility
steps.detail: Records who requested which action via console, CLI, SDK or API.

steps.label: Manage access
steps.detail: Right people, right resources, right times, right reasons.

exam_angles.q: A healthcare provider plans to move its patient records system to a public cloud PaaS. Patient data must stay in the country, and the regulator wants proof of who accessed which record. Propose the security architecture and say which duties remain the provider's.

items: **Placement**: **classify patient data**, use an **in-country region**, confirm the **PaaS responsibility split**
**Encryption**: **TLS** in transit and encrypt **at rest**; decide **who holds and can use the keys**, since **BYOK** and **customer-held keys** differ
**Access**: **least-privilege identities** for **users and services**; **mask or tokenise identifiers** in **non-clinical views**
**Edge**: a **WAF** and **provider DDoS protection** in front
**For the regulator**: retain **protected audit events** and **database activity monitoring per record**

sub: **Classification**, **access decisions** and **accountability** stay with the **healthcare provider**

exam_angles.q: A misconfigured storage bucket leaked customer data. The provider's service worked as documented. Using the shared responsibility model, explain who is accountable, then give a cause, a countermeasure and its drawback.

items: **Provider** secures the **storage service** itself; the **customer** secures **what is in it**, including **configuration**, **access control** and **data classification**, just as with the **firewall example**
**Countermeasure**: define **bucket policies** in **reviewed IaC**, **block public access by default**, and **alert on policy changes**
**Drawback**: **slower changes** and **friction** for teams that legitimately **publish public content**

exam_angles.q: A microservices application exposes 30 public APIs, and its developers keep cloud keys in config files. Pick three Treacherous Twelve threats most relevant here, explain each through STRIDE, and give mitigations.

sub: **Authenticate and authorise every call**, **validate input**, **rate-limit**, add a **WAF**

items.t: **Insufficient identity, credential and access management** (**spoofing**, **elevation of privilege**)
sub: Move keys to a **secrets manager** and **rotate** them
Use **least-privilege roles** and **scan repositories** for secrets

a.foot: Throughout: run **DevSecOps scanning** of **code and images**, and keep **audit trails** to address **repudiation**.

exam_angles.q: Design data protection across the full lifecycle for a fintech's customer documents (ID scans, statements), including how deletion requests are honoured.

items: **Store**: **encrypt** with **controlled key use**, **restrict access**, **back up** and **monitor**
**Share**: **TLS**, **VPN** or **SSH** channels, and **DLP** or **rights controls** for **external parties**

sub: Only works if **backups**, **logs** and **analytics copies** hold **no plaintext** and the **keys are truly destroyed**

a.foot: **Access follows classification** at every stage.

exam_angles.q: A bank's board asks whether to use public, private or hybrid cloud 'for security'. Argue that the deployment model alone doesn't decide this, and recommend an approach.

a.lead: The **deployment model alone** doesn't decide security.
items: **Security depends on** **data location**, **access control**, **key management**, **provider duties** and **recovery**, not on the **label**
**Public cloud** can meet **sensitive requirements**; **private cloud** still needs all of these controls
**Hybrid** if specific data must **legally stay on premises**: **controlled, encrypted connectivity** and **tokenisation** so public-cloud services handle **tokens rather than raw data**
a.foot: Either way, the **bank keeps responsibility** for **data classification** and **access**.

exam_angles.q: Your organisation detected a breach only after 200 days, through a customer complaint. Diagnose the gaps and propose the monitoring, visibility and access capabilities you would add, with the main cost.

items: **Gaps**: no meaningful **alerting**, little **audit coverage**, and probably **stale or over-broad access**
**Monitoring**: **continuous monitoring** with alerts on **unusual data movement** and **database access**
**Visibility**: **audit events** for **identity and resource actions** with **protected, long retention**, and an **incident response process**
a.foot: **Main cost** is **ongoing**: **storing logs** and **triaging alerts** needs **staff**, and **noisy alerts get ignored**, so tune them to the **valuable data first**.
